text: It's worth clarifying a subtle distinction between Effect.succeed and Effect.sync. With succeed, the value is captured when the effect is first created. If we pass in new Date(), it will once and forever return that exact Date. When we run it, we'll get the original Date. Try again later, same Date. Tomorrow? That same God-forsaken Date. With sync, the computation is suspended within a thunk. When we run it, the thunk is called, and we get a brand new Date. When we run it again, it's re-executed, and we get another pristine Date.
code:
import { Effect } from "effect"

const getDate = Effect.succeed(new Date())
